pois.visitTips: Boaters can anchor off Julian Bay in stable weather, or use the NPS dock at Presque Isle Bay on the sheltered west side and hike the short boardwalk across to Julian Bay. The 3-mile Tombolo Trail explores the dune ridges and bog; stay on boardwalks in wetland sections. The excursion boat and water taxis also serve Stockton in season.
funFacts: The tombolo is the only landform of its kind in Wisconsin, joining former Presque Isle island to Stockton with a 6,000-year-old sand bridge
The singing comes from uniform, rounded quartz grains shearing against each other — it works best in dry sand on warm days
The tombolo complex holds bogs, dunes, lagoons, savannas, and pines, plus the park's largest campground at Presque Isle Bay

pois.name: Outer Island Sandspit
pois.tagline: A mile and a half of wild sand trailing off the archipelago's outermost island
pois.story:
Off the southern tip of Outer Island, the archipelago's most exposed island tapers into a magnificent sandspit — about a mile and a half of open sand, beach, and low dunes reaching into Lake Superior. Currents wrapping around the island's flanks meet in its lee and drop their cargo of sand eroded from clay bluffs up-shore, building one of the finest examples of a sandspit in the entire park and a highlight of the state's Apostle Islands Sandscapes natural-area designation.

The spit is a living landform, reshaped by every gale, and its plants are specialists in instability: beach grass, beach pea, wormwood, and mats of creeping juniper stitch the dunes together. It is also a landfall for migrating birds funneling along the islands — and a lonely, glorious campsite location, with the 7.5-mile Sandspit Trail linking the south-end campsites to the 1874 lighthouse at the island's north tip.

For boaters, the spit is the classic staging point for weather windows at the park's outer edge; for paddlers it is a hard-won reward at the end of some of the most committing crossings in the Apostles.
pois.visitTips: Anchor in the lee of the spit according to wind direction; holding is sand. Campsites sit near the spit at the island's south end (permits required). Respect any roped-off or posted plover nesting areas in early summer, camp only at designated sites, and avoid trampling dune vegetation. The Sandspit Trail runs 7.5 miles north to the Outer Island Light.
funFacts: The spit is about 1.5 miles long — one of only two true sandspits in the park (Cat Island has the other)
Beach pea, a nitrogen-fixer, helps fertilize the nutrient-poor sand so later dune plants can take hold
Endangered piping plovers have nested in the park only on Long Island and at Outer Island's protected beaches — heed any posted closures on the spit

pois.name: Outer Island Old-Growth Forest
pois.tagline: A cathedral of ancient hemlock the loggers — and the deer — never touched
pois.story:
On Outer Island's northern tip, near the 1874 lighthouse, stands one of the best surviving pieces of old-growth northern hardwood-hemlock forest in the upper Great Lakes: a 202-acre remnant of towering hemlock, white pine, yellow birch, and cedar, threaded with clay-bank seeps and ephemeral ponds. While nearly every island in the Apostles was cut over in the logging era, this far corner of the farthest island escaped, and walking beneath it feels like stepping back before the axe — sunlight falling through the canopy in shafts, the understory open and hushed.

What makes the stand scientifically precious is an absence: deer. Without browsing pressure, hemlock and Canada yew regenerate here as they rarely can on the mainland, making Outer Island a reference forest — a baseline for what the Northwoods looked like and how it renews itself. The area is protected within the Apostle Islands Maritime Forests State Natural Area and the Gaylord Nelson Wilderness.
pois.visitTips: Reach the north end via the lighthouse dock area (landing is weather-dependent and exposed) or hike the 7.5-mile Sandspit Trail from the south-end campsites. Travel is primitive wilderness hiking — no facilities beyond the light station area. Leave no trace; the seeps and ephemeral ponds are fragile.
funFacts: The 202-acre stand is considered one of the best old-growth hemlock-hardwood examples left in the upper Great Lakes
Because Outer Island lacks deer, browse-sensitive species like Canada yew and hemlock seedlings thrive here — a rarity across the region
The forest shares the island's north tip with the tallest brick lighthouse in the Apostles (1874)

pois.name: Raspberry Island Sandspit
pois.tagline: A protected sand point and favorite anchorage below the showplace lighthouse
pois.story:
Off Raspberry Island's southwest corner, a neat cuspate sandspit hooks into the West Channel — one of a family of wedge-shaped sand forelands the currents have built on the lee corners of the Apostles. The spit shelters a popular small-boat anchorage, and its beach and low dunes carry the classic pioneer plant community of the islands: beach grass and nitrogen-fixing beach pea binding bare sand into ridges that shrubs and pines can later claim.

The island above it has an unusual ecological backstory. Because Raspberry was a U.S. Lighthouse Service reservation, it was never commercially logged, and today parts of it fall within the Apostle Islands Yew Forest State Natural Area — protecting Canada yew thickets that deer have wiped out across most of the mainland Northwoods. To keep the fragile spit vegetation intact, the park bars camping on the sandspit and lighthouse grounds; boats anchor off the spit while day visitors climb the stairs to tour the restored 1906 lighthouse, long billed as the showplace of the Apostle Islands.
pois.visitTips: Powerboats and sailboats commonly anchor overnight off the sandspit; a small first-come dock below the lighthouse serves day visitors. Camping is prohibited on the sandspit and lighthouse grounds — primitive camping only elsewhere on the island. NPS rangers lead summer lighthouse tours; the spit's dune plants are fragile, so walk on bare sand and established paths.
funFacts: Raspberry's spit is a textbook cuspate foreland — the park counts similar sand wedges on ten of its islands
The island escaped commercial logging entirely because it belonged to the U.S. Lighthouse Service
Parts of Raspberry are in the Apostle Islands Yew Forest State Natural Area (designated 2010), sheltering Canada yew that deer browsing has erased elsewhere

pois.name: Michigan Island Lagoon & Sandspit
pois.tagline: A driftwood-strewn spit hiding a secret marshy lagoon
pois.story:
At Michigan Island's western end, about nine-tenths of a mile from the island's two lighthouses, a long sandspit sweeps into the lake — sweeping dunes, wave-polished driftwood, and clear water shading from gold to deep blue. Tucked just inland behind the spit lies a quiet, marshy lagoon, one of the sheltered wetlands that form when a growing sand barrier seals off a corner of the lake and lets a still-water world develop behind it: frog song, dragonflies, and waterbirds a stone's throw from open Superior.

The spit is also the island's landing and camping zone. Boats beach on the sand or anchor off and dinghy in, and a single campsite hides behind the dunes in the trees, reached by a boardwalk from a marker on the beach. From the spit, a trail leads up to the light station — the odd couple of an 1857 stone lighthouse built here by mistake and the 112-foot steel tower that replaced it in 1929, the tallest light in the Apostles.
pois.visitTips: Land small boats directly on the spit's sand or anchor off and dinghy ashore; enter the dunes only at the marked boardwalk. The single campsite (permit required) is set in the trees behind the dunes. Walk quietly to the lagoon edge for herons and waterfowl — footing is marshy. A trail connects the spit to the lighthouses for a climbable-tower view when staff are present.
funFacts: The lagoon behind the spit is a textbook barrier-built wetland — sand seals off a bay corner, and a marsh ecosystem develops in the stillness behind it
Michigan Island's first lighthouse (1857) was built on the wrong island; its 1929 replacement tower is the tallest in the archipelago
The campsite sits 0.9 mile west of the light station, behind the dunes — campers must use the site, not the beach

pois.name: Big Bay Lagoon & Barrier Beach
pois.tagline: A 1.5-mile sand crescent sealing off a lagoon and a floating sphagnum bog
pois.story:
On Madeline Island's east shore, Big Bay shows what 15,000 years of patient wave-work can do. When the island emerged from beneath the last glacier, Big Bay was an open, shallow arm of the lake; longshore currents then built a barrier beach across its middle and later a second baymouth bar across its entrance, trapping the water behind. The result today is a mile-and-a-half crescent of sand backed by Big Bay Lagoon and an extensive quaking sphagnum-sedge bog — a whole northern wetland world hidden a dune's width from Lake Superior surf.

The 963-acre spit-and-bog complex is protected as the DNR-owned Big Bay Sand Spit and Bog State Natural Area, its barrier beach shared between Big Bay State Park and the town park. Old beach ridges behind the modern strand record earlier stands of the lake, and the bog mat — carnivorous plants, orchids, and all — literally trembles underfoot where boardwalks cross it. Note for trip-planners: Madeline Island lies outside Apostle Islands National Lakeshore; this one belongs to the Wisconsin State Park system and the Town of La Pointe.

For boaters and paddlers, the beach is one of the sweetest swim stops on the lake — Big Bay's shallows warm faster than almost any water in the Apostles — and the lagoon rewards a slow kayak or SUP lap along its dark, tannin-stained edges.
pois.visitTips: Reach Madeline Island by ferry from Bayfield, then drive about 7 miles to Big Bay State Park (vehicle admission required) or Big Bay Town Park at the lagoon outlet. Kayaks/SUPs can launch into the lagoon from the town-park side; the barrier beach is a 1.5-mile walk-and-swim paradise. Stay on boardwalks over the bog, and expect warmer swimming here than anywhere in the outer islands.
funFacts: Big Bay Lagoon began as an open bay of Lake Superior; two successive sand barriers — one mid-bay, one across the mouth — sealed it off after the glaciers left
The 963-acre Big Bay Sand Spit and Bog is State Natural Area No. 156, with a quaking bog mat that ripples when you walk the boardwalk
Madeline Island is the one large Apostle outside the national lakeshore — Big Bay is managed by Big Bay State Park (est. 1963) and the adjacent town park

pois.name: Eagle Island Bird Sanctuary (Closed to Landing)
pois.tagline: The Apostles' only great blue heron rookery — admire from offshore
pois.story:
Tiny Eagle Island — about 20 acres of rock and trees off the archipelago's western edge, due north of the mainland sea caves — is a nursery, not a destination. It is the only island in the Apostles where great blue herons nest, and its trees and shores also host colonies of double-crested cormorants and herring gulls. Together with Gull Island at the opposite end of the park, it accounts for the great majority of the lakeshore's breeding herring gulls — a striking share of the entire Wisconsin Lake Superior shore's population.

Because colonial waterbirds abandon nests wholesale when disturbed, the island is closed to public entry, with the strictest protections during the nesting season from late spring through early September; it has been part of the Apostle Islands Critical Species State Natural Area since 1992, and researchers visit only for annual bird surveys. For boaters, the reward is the view: pass well offshore on a calm evening and watch herons commute like slow pterodactyls between the island and mainland marshes.
pois.visitTips: Landing is prohibited; the island and an offshore buffer are closed during the nesting season (roughly late May through early September) — check current NPS closures before your trip. View from a boat standing well off; disturbance that flushes birds can doom eggs and chicks to gulls and weather. Best viewing is early morning or evening when herons are commuting.
funFacts: Eagle and Gull islands together hold roughly 88 percent of the lakeshore's breeding herring gulls
Eagle is the archipelago's only great blue heron rookery
The island sits almost due north of the Mawikwe Bay sea caves — an easy offshore detour for cave-bound paddlers, binoculars in hand

pois.name: Gull Island Bird Sanctuary (Closed to Landing)
pois.tagline: Three treeless acres that raise most of the lakeshore's gulls
pois.story:
Off Michigan Island's northeastern tip lies the smallest of the Apostles: Gull Island, a flat, three-acre shelf of rock barely shrugging above the lake. Its poverty is its power — with no trees, no cover, and crucially no mammalian predators, it is the most important gullery in the archipelago, packed each summer with nesting herring gulls (and, in some years, ring-billed gulls), while the surrounding shoals double as important fish spawning grounds. A small navigational light marks the island for passing boats.

Together with Eagle Island 30 miles to the west, this speck supports the bulk of the lakeshore's — and much of Wisconsin's Lake Superior — breeding herring gulls. Like Eagle, it is part of the Apostle Islands Critical Species State Natural Area and is closed to visitors so the colony can nest undisturbed. Boaters should give it a respectful berth in season; the reward is the spectacle of a full colony wheeling and crying over a rock you could walk across in a minute.
pois.visitTips: Closed to landing year-round to protect nesting colonies; observe from a boat well offshore, especially May through early September. Shoal water surrounds the island — give it navigational as well as ecological clearance. Binoculars from the Michigan Island sandspit area also give good colony views in flight.
funFacts: At about 3 acres, Gull is the smallest named island in the Apostles — and pound for pound its most productive bird habitat
Its shoals are an important spawning site for Lake Superior fish, feeding the very colony above
The island's lack of mammal predators is exactly why the gulls chose it — a moat 20 miles wide

pois.name: Island Black Bears (Oak, Stockton & Sand)
pois.tagline: Blueberry-fed swimmers with some of the densest bear country in Wisconsin
pois.story:
The Apostles' most surprising residents may be their black bears. Strong swimmers, bears paddle the channels between the mainland and the islands, and three islands — Oak, Stockton, and Sand — support their own resident populations. DNA studies using hair snagged on barbed-wire stations revealed four distinct genetic groups (Stockton, Sand, Oak, and mainland ancestry), evidence that island bears aren't just passing through: they're locals, raising cubs on berry flats and beach ridges surrounded by the world's largest lake.

The numbers are remarkable. Stockton's population grew from a single pair in the 1970s to 31 bears by 1994 — for years billed as one of the densest black bear populations in North America — before declining by half by 2010. Meanwhile Oak Island took the crown: about 18 bears at roughly 0.88 bears per square kilometer, the highest density reported in Wisconsin, with Sand Island close behind at 0.85. For campers this is bear country in miniature — same rules, smaller wilderness: food lockers, clean camps, and no snacks in the tent.
pois.visitTips: On Oak, Stockton, and Sand islands, store all food, trash, and scented items in provided bear lockers or hard-sided containers — never in tents. Cook away from your sleeping area, pack out garbage, and never approach or feed a bear. Paddlers should also stow food overnight when beach-camping on nearby islands: bears swim.
funFacts: Oak Island's bear density (about 0.88 bears/km² in 2010) was the highest reported anywhere in Wisconsin, with Sand Island nearly equal
Stockton went from two bears in the 1970s to 31 by 1994 — then lost half its population, and 84 percent of its females, by 2010
Genetic testing shows island bears form distinct populations — bears born on Stockton or Sand carry no ancestry from other islands

pois.name: Long Island–Chequamegon Point Piping Plover Refuge
pois.tagline: Wisconsin's last stronghold of the Great Lakes piping plover
pois.story:
Long Island isn't really an island — it's a low barrier spit of pure sand, the only one in the park, arcing between Chequamegon Bay and open Lake Superior with no bedrock underneath. It has flickered between island and peninsula many times as storms cut and currents heal it; since the mid-1970s it has been connected to the mainland near the Bad River delta. The Ojibwe call it Zaagawaamikong-neyaashi, and the adjacent peninsula lands belong to the Bad River Band, whose crews help guard its most precious residents.

Those residents are Great Lakes piping plovers — small, sand-colored shorebirds so endangered that the entire Great Lakes population once fell to a few dozen pairs. Long Island/Chequamegon Point is the only place in Wisconsin where they have regularly nested since the 1970s, and the NPS acquired the island in 1986 partly to protect them. It is federally designated critical habitat; each summer, biologists cage individual nests with predator exclosures ringed by wide twine perimeters, and stretches of beach close to landings while chicks — improbable sand-colored puffballs on toothpick legs — learn to forage the swash line.

Two lighthouses share the spit with the plovers near its western tip, including the skeletal Chequamegon Point light, moved 100 feet inland in 1987 as the beach eroded beneath it — a reminder that this whole landform is permanently on the move.
pois.visitTips: Portions of the beach close during nesting season (birds arrive late April–early May; closures typically run into August) — land only outside posted areas, keep dogs off entirely, and give exclosures a wide berth. The spit is shoal-fringed; approach in shallow-draft boats with care. Two campsites exist on the island but check current closures first; the Bad River Band's adjacent lands are not open to public use.
funFacts: Long Island is the park's only barrier spit — sand all the way down, with no bedrock core — and has repeatedly switched between island and peninsula
It is Wisconsin's only regular piping plover nesting site since the 1970s and part of federally designated critical habitat (2001)
Nests are protected by metal predator exclosures about 12 feet across, ringed by twine perimeters roughly 100 feet wide

pois.name: La Pointe Historic Core & Madeline Island Museum
pois.tagline: The fur-trade capital where the 1854 Treaty of La Pointe was signed
pois.story:
In 1835 the American Fur Company gave up its cramped post at Madeline Island's southern end and built a whole new La Pointe on the deeper harbor of Sandy Bay — wharf, fur and fish storehouses, and employee housing — launching its schooner John Jacob Astor that August. For a few years this was the company's inland headquarters: 280 packs of furs shipped out in August 1835, and as the fur trade faded, barrels of salted whitefish and trout took their place — 320 barrels on hand by January 1836.

On September 30, 1854, in front of trader Charles Oakes' long frame house — remembered ever after as Treaty Hall — leaders of the Lake Superior Ojibwe signed the Treaty of La Pointe with U.S. commissioners Henry Gilbert and David Herriman. The Ojibwe negotiated from strength, refusing to cede the mineral-rich north shore until the government guaranteed permanent reservations in their homelands. The treaty created the Bad River and Red Cliff reservations and reserved a roughly 200-acre fishing ground on Madeline Island itself. It capped Chief Buffalo's extraordinary 1852 journey to Washington, made in his nineties, that overturned the federal removal order.

Fire took most of old La Pointe — the fur company buildings in 1869, Father Baraga's church in 1901, Treaty Hall itself in 1923. But in 1958 summer residents Leo and Bella Capser joined four salvaged log buildings, including one of the last American Fur Company structures, into the Madeline Island Historical Museum near the ferry dock, seeded with island trapper Al Galazen's artifact collection and run since 1968 by the Wisconsin Historical Society.
funFacts: Treaty Hall was donated to the D.A.R. as a museum in 1917 — and burned down in 1923.
The museum's four joined log buildings include the old town jail and the Old Sailors' Home, built by Olaf Anderson in memory of his brother who drowned in Lake Superior.
Fourteen chiefs and headmen signed the 1854 treaty for the La Pointe bands, led by Chief Buffalo (Kechewaishke).
pois.visitTips: Tie up at the La Pointe marina or ride the Madeline Island Ferry from Bayfield; the museum sits a short walk from the ferry landing and is open seasonally. The Ojibwe Memorial Park and historic cemetery are nearby — treat them as the sacred ground they are.

pois.name: Old Mission Site, Madeline Island
pois.tagline: A vanished mission village that became one of the lake's beloved resorts
pois.story:
In the fall of 1834 Protestant missionary Sherman Hall began a two-story log mission house on shoreline about halfway between Michel Cadotte's old trading post and the fur company's new village — school, church, and residence all under one roof. Florantha Sproat taught the mission school while Hall translated the New Testament into Ojibwe. Father Frederic Baraga's rival Catholic mission, arriving in 1835, baptized 148 converts by that October; the Protestants, who demanded years of rigorous study first, counted only seven or eight Ojibwe and metis members across three decades. The mission was abandoned in the 1850s after most La Pointe Ojibwe moved to Bad River and Red Cliff.

In 1897 the Reverend Edward P. Salmon of Beloit bought the tract, renovated the old building, added a dining room and dormitories, and even moved La Pointe's Protestant church onto the grounds. His Old Mission Inn — lights out at 10 p.m. — became a catalyst for Madeline Island's whole summer colony: around 1906 he built about a dozen cottages for returning St. Paul families, and guests who fell in love with the island went on to build Nebraska Row and the island's other cottage enclaves.

Salmon's nephew gave the property to Beloit College in 1941; the college sold it in 1953, and in the mid-1960s the old mission building was demolished. One delightful fragment survived: part of the Old Mission Inn's dining room lives on today as the La Pointe post office.
funFacts: The relocated Protestant church, one of Wisconsin's oldest religious buildings, collapsed on the mission grounds in 1943.
In the 1920s the inn's apple and cherry orchard was replaced with a tennis court and golf course.
Colonel Frederick Woods found his 1897 cottage on the mission grounds too rustic and the rules too strict — so he built north of the village and founded Nebraska Row instead.
pois.visitTips: The mission site lies along the western shore south of La Pointe village (position approximate; the land is private, so enjoy it from the water). The surviving post-office fragment is in the village itself.

pois.name: Bayfield–La Pointe Ice Road & Windsled Crossing
pois.island: North Channel between Bayfield and Madeline Island
pois.tagline: The highway that appears every winter — and the school bus that grows propellers
pois.story:
Madeline Island is the only Apostle island with a year-round town, and every winter the two-mile channel to Bayfield becomes its lifeline and its hazard. By January 1872 a local account already called ice travel between the two towns 'quite extensive' — pedestrians, dog teams, horse-drawn sleighs, and iceboats, one said to move 'like a red hot locomotive.' In March 1871 Jim Brown sailed a hand sled rigged with a double blanket down the shore from the Sioux River to Bayfield; missionary Father Chebul famously lost his way on the ice that same year, undone by wind, drifting snow, and his own near-sightedness. The crossing could kill: in April 1915 a small boat returning from Bayfield capsized in an ice field and three of the five men aboard drowned.

The islanders' answer, from the 1940s on, was pure ingenuity: the windsled, pioneered by Harry Nelson and the Russell brothers of La Pointe — a flat-bottomed hull built from boat and airplane parts, pushed by huge propeller fans, able to skim over ice too thin for trucks and to float if it breaks through. Windsleds took over the mail run and, crucially, the school run: island students in the upper grades attend school in Bayfield, and after a state senator argued that a windsled is simply a big yellow school bus, a federal transportation grant delivered a purpose-built 9,000-pound, twenty-seat windsled in 2000.

Once the channel locks in, a plowed lane — legally an extension of County Highway H, marked with a double line of discarded Christmas trees — carries cars and trucks over the lake. The rhythm continues today: ferry, then windsled through freeze-up, then the ice road, then windsled again at break-up. Climate is rewriting the story, though — one longtime islander's fifty years of records show seasons shrinking from more than ninety days of open road toward winters when the road never opens at all. When you cross this channel by boat in July, you are on the main street of a town that exists only in winter.
funFacts: In 1898 an enterprising saloon operated out on the Chequamegon Bay ice halfway between Ashland and Washburn — neatly beyond the reach of the city's $500 license fee.
The ice road is officially an extension of County Highway H — speed and weight limits apply on the lake, and retired Christmas trees mark the safe lane.
The windsled ride is famously loud and bumpy — locals treat it as part commute, part carnival ride.
pois.visitTips: A summer boater will only see open water here, but you are crossing the winter highway: the ferry lane you follow between Bayfield and La Pointe is the same route the windsled and ice road take in January. Keep clear of the Madeline Island ferries and watch for traffic.

pois.name: Bayfield Fishing Waterfront & the Booth Fisheries Era
pois.tagline: Home port of the Lake Superior 'fish trust' — where a million pounds of fish froze on lake-cut ice
pois.story:
By 1885 Bayfield was the leading commercial fishing port on Lake Superior — more commercial fishermen than any other port on the lake — its waterfront crowded with the Boutin family's boats and a swarm of smaller dealers. That year Chicago's A. Booth and Sons arrived on a trial basis, and the Bayfield Businessmen's Association sealed the deal by donating a lakefront dock site in the center of town. Booth built packinghouses, net sheds, ice houses, and a freezing plant whose four freezers could hold nearly a million pounds and freeze 10,000 pounds of fish a day. Booth's gill-net steamers expanded island fishing on an industrial scale, and its collecting steamer made the rounds of fish camps from Sand to Outer Island. Many fishermen sold on shares or carried Booth debt and called it being 'tied up to Booth.' In 1898 the firm incorporated as A. Booth and Company — a $5.5 million corporation known across the lakes as the fish trust.

All that fish ran on ice cut from the lake itself. Late each winter Booth put forty men on Chequamegon Bay to harvest twenty-two hundred tons of ice — blocks of several hundred pounds sawed free offshore, rafted through channels cut in the ice, hauled up chutes by horses, and stacked in insulated ice houses to last the summer. Even after dealer Howard Elmore installed a state-of-the-art twenty-ton Frick refrigerator in 1928, he still sent twenty-five men onto the ice to cut eight hundred tons — machine ice alone could not keep up with the herring.

In 1938 Booth launched the Apostle Islands, a diesel boat built to collect fish and carry sightseers at the same time ('A day of complete relaxation on Lake Superior will do wonders for your morale'). Then the sea lamprey ended the era: between 1950 and 1960 the lake trout catch fell about 90 percent, and in 1958 Booth — the last dealer still sending a collecting boat around the island camps — stopped the run. The barrel-making shop survives as the NRHP-listed Booth Cooperage at the north end of the waterfront, while Bodin Fisheries and the Red Cliff Fish Company keep Bayfield's fishing tradition alive.
funFacts: Barrels assembled at the Booth Cooperage were packed with salted fish for rail shipment after the railroad reached Bayfield in 1883.
In the early 1870s fish dealer J. B. Bono shipped Bayfield fish to St. Paul by dogsled.
Booth's dual-purpose boat Apostle Islands alternated western and eastern island routes six days a week, hauling fish and tourists together until 1958.
pois.visitTips: Stand on the Bayfield city dock at the foot of Rittenhouse Avenue — the donated 'lakefront site in the center of town.' The old Booth site and cooperage sit at the north end of the working waterfront (the cooperage now houses a kayak outfitter), and the Bayfield Maritime Museum is a block away. Pair with the Hokenson Brothers Fishery at Little Sand Bay for the family-scale version.

pois.name: Houghton: The Vanished Quarry Town
pois.tagline: A company town that tried to out-obelisk Cleopatra's Needle
pois.story:
In 1888 Frederick Prentice — who had been buying Chequamegon Bay stone lands since the 1850s — organized the Prentice Brownstone Company and opened a quarry at Houghton Point, north of Washburn. One hundred men were at work by that October and more than two hundred by 1890, making it by far the region's largest quarry. Around it grew an entire town of Houghton: workers' cottages, boardinghouses, a general store, a blacksmith shop, and two sawmills — one for lumber, one for slicing sandstone. Output climbed from 383,887 cubic feet in 1889 to 623,334 in 1890.

Prentice's grandest stunt came in 1892: a single brownstone obelisk for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition — 115 feet tall, ten feet square at the base, over four hundred tons, deliberately taller than Cleopatra's Needle in New York. No lake vessel or railcar could carry it, so a special scow was designed. Then the Panic of 1893 struck, the plan collapsed, and the mighty monolith was eventually cut up for ordinary building stone. Prentice sent four 25-foot monoliths to Chicago instead, including a statue of an Ojibwe chief and a Wisconsin badger.

Concrete finished what the panic started: the regional brownstone industry was essentially dead by 1903, and the town of Houghton faded back into the woods. Washburn still calls itself the Monolith City, and its brownstone bank and public buildings are the town's lasting monument.
funFacts: Houghton Point stone was chosen for the monolith because it was free of clay pockets, tints, and streaks.
The Bank of Washburn (1889) was built of brownstone quarried at Houghton Point.
Prentice also built the fanciful Cedar Bark Cottage on Hermit Island — which, legend says, his young wife took one look at and refused to inhabit.
pois.visitTips: Cruise close along Houghton Point's ledges between Washburn and Bayfield to spot quarried faces; Houghton Falls State Natural Area, just inland, makes a good shore excursion from Washburn's marina.

pois.name: Trout Point Logging Camp
pois.tagline: A frozen-in-time lumber camp on Stockton's wild northeast shore
pois.story:
The John Schroeder Lumber Company of Milwaukee opened its main assault on Stockton Island's timber in the fall of 1912, building three big camps and putting nearly 250 men to work the first winter. By 1914-15 three hundred men were cutting hemlock, hardwood, and cedar — about ten million board feet that season — hauled by sleigh over iced roads, then rafted and scowed across to Schroeder's Ashland mill each summer. It was the largest logging operation the islands had yet seen.

Island logging meant island isolation. In January 1913 two men lay with broken limbs for days while rotten ice blocked the doctor's crossing; so many loggers quit over the medical risk that Schroeder began stationing a physician on the island through freeze-up and break-up. Feeding the camps was solved with frontier directness: several hundred hogs and cattle were shipped out to roam Stockton freely and were slaughtered as needed — 569 head of cattle added in 1917 alone.

The Trout Point camp on the northeast shore, occupied about 1912-1920, is the best-preserved logging camp in the islands. Archaeologists in 1982 mapped thirty-six features — kitchen, dining hall, root cellar, two bunkhouses sleeping fifty-six men each, filer's shack, and office/store — with tableware, tobacco tins, and even part of a harmonica lying where the loggers left them. Animal bones show the men ate more beef than pork. Schroeder cut the last of Stockton's timber in the spring of 1920, and the site joined the National Register in 1988.
funFacts: In February 1914 newspapers claimed five hundred men were working for Schroeder on Stockton Island.
Tools were too valuable to abandon — archaeologists found only a cant hook, a saw, and a wedge.
When fisherman John Nelson built his Stockton camp in 1919, he salvaged boards from the freshly abandoned Trout Point buildings.
pois.visitTips: There is no dock on the northeast shore; most visitors reach Trout Point on foot via the trail from Presque Isle Bay. The camp is an archaeological site — take photographs, leave every artifact in place.

pois.name: South Twin Fishing Village & Trollers Home Resort
pois.tagline: The island kingdom of 'King Lenus' and its fifty-cent resort
pois.story:
South Twin's protected west-side harbor made it a favorite fish-camp island by the 1910s, when Charlie Benson, John Fried, Olaf Edwards, Henry Johnson Sr., Lenus Jacobson, and John Duva all fished from its shore. Benson had been shoreman at Booth's company camp here until Booth closed it around 1908. Summers brought whole families: every year Fredrekke Benson ferried two cows to the island, churning butter, making cheese, and selling milk to the other fish-camp families.

In 1931 hired-man-made-good Lenus Jacobson traveled to Minneapolis and bought the entire island from the Willey family for $975. He promptly raised rents and told the other fishermen where they could set their nets — behavior that earned him the nickname 'King Lenus' and triggered an exodus: one by one, Fried, Edwards, and Benson dismantled their camps and moved across the channel to Rocky Island. Left with empty cabins, Lenus and his wife Inga turned them into the Trollers Home: bed, sheets, and firewood for fifty cents a night, no meals, and a main cabin boasting gas-powered electricity and an electric washing machine.

Carl Moe and George Englund of Bayfield added a restaurant and reopened it as Trollers Home Resort in May 1946 — eighty fish dinners served on opening day — but sea lamprey, foul weather, and competition from the Rocky Island Air Haven across the channel doomed it, and they sold in 1951. Later owner John Atwood platted vacation lots that never materialized. Today second-growth forest is reclaiming the island, and John Duva's log cabin from the 1910s is the only fish-camp building left standing.
funFacts: South Twin is the only island in the national lakeshore with no rock outcropping anywhere on its shoreline.
Charter captains once ended fishing days here with a fish dinner and an overnight stay for their clients.
A former airstrip clearing at the island's southwest end is still reachable by a half-mile trail from the dock.
pois.visitTips: An NPS dock on the west side gives easy access; the old resort clearing and Duva cabin (used by NPS for storage — view from outside only) are near the landing, directly facing Rocky Island. Good lee anchorage from easterlies between South Twin and Rocky.

pois.name: Armstrong's Landing & the Camp of the 'King of Oak Island'
pois.tagline: One sandspit, two legends: Chief Buffalo's adopted son, then a hermit king
pois.story:
The sandspit at Oak Island's southwest corner is the best natural landing on the island, and history used it twice over. In 1855 the trader Benjamin Armstrong — adopted son of Chief Buffalo (Kechewaishke) and the interpreter who accompanied the Ojibwe leader's famous 1852 delegation to Washington — moved his family here from La Pointe. He built a house, barn, and dock, cleared forty acres, and ran a trading post and wood yard, selling hardwood fuel to passing steamboats and trading with the Ojibwe until 1861. Government surveyors described his house, dock, and clearing in their 1856-57 notes, and a Bayfield newspaper in 1860 marveled at his seven-foot-six-inch rye. It was Armstrong, too, who witnessed the hermit Wilson count out his coin hoard across the water on Hermit Island.

Decades later the same bank above the sandspit held logging Camp 3 (site 47AS64), used by R. D. Pike and later the Stearns Lumber Company. When the loggers left, Martin Kane moved into the filer's shack — the solitary fisherman the Ashland Daily Press crowned 'the King of Oak Island.' Kane had logged and captained fishing boats here before following his wife to the Seattle shipyards; after her death he returned around 1920 and lived alone in the islands until he died in 1947, keeping a garden and orchard and living on fish, venison, and bear meat.

The king's self-sufficiency nearly killed him: one winter, weakened by anemia, he hitched his dogs to a sled and let them pull him across the ice to the mainland, spending weeks in an Ashland hospital. Yet visitors found him unfailingly hospitable, and Bayfield liked him well. Archaeologists have mapped a dozen possible structures on the old camp site — look, but leave every artifact where it lies.
funFacts: Government surveyors in the 1850s also recorded an Ojibwe maple-sugar camp in the middle of Oak Island — the sugar bush still exists today.
Martin Kane twice fell through winter ice and both times managed to roll out of the water and back onto the ice.
After his anemia scare, Kane treated himself with self-administered injections of liver extract at his island cabin.
pois.visitTips: Anchor off or land at the sandspit on Oak Island's south/southwest corner (NPS campsite 1 sits on the spit at 46.9144, -90.7362). The old camp remains on the bank above are a protected archaeological site — take photographs, not souvenirs.
sources: John B. Chapple, 'There's Still a King in U.S.; He's Martin Kane, the King of Oak Island,' The Wisconsin Islands (Ashland Daily Press, 1945), cited in NPS Historic Resource Study
Eleanor Knight, 'Martin Kane, King of Oak Island,' Bayfield County Press, March 6, 1958, cited in NPS Historic Resource Study
Benjamin G. Armstrong, Early Life Among the Indians (1892), cited in NPS Historic Resource Study

pois.name: Ira H. Owen — Lost with All Hands, 1905
pois.tagline: The Mataafa Storm's only total loss — a steel steamer that vanished east of Outer Island and has never been found
pois.story:
The Ira H. Owen came off the ways at Cleveland's Globe Iron Works in 1887, one of the very first steel freighters on the Great Lakes. On the morning of November 28, 1905, she cleared Duluth on her last run of the season with nineteen crew and a light load of 116,000 bushels of barley — steaming straight into the worst blow in Lake Superior's recorded history. The Mataafa Storm drove winds past seventy miles an hour with temperatures below zero; roughly thirty vessels were caught and battered on the lake in those three days.

East of Outer Island, at the height of the storm, Captain Alva Keller of the freighter Harold B. Nye sighted the Owen struggling and blowing distress signals. The Nye, badly damaged herself and having lost a man overboard, could do nothing. A snow squall closed between the two ships; when it lifted two hours later, the Owen was simply gone. Three days later the Sir William Siemens steamed through a field of wreckage twelve miles east of Michigan Island — chairs, the top of a cabin, life preservers stenciled 'S.S. Ira H. Owen.' No bodies were ever recovered.

She was the only vessel lost with all hands in the Mataafa Storm, and the wreck has never been located. The Wisconsin Historical Society believes she most likely lies in deep water off Outer Island. This marker is symbolic: the true resting place of the Owen and her nineteen men remains one of Lake Superior's unsolved mysteries.
funFacts: The Owen was the only ship lost with all hands among the roughly thirty vessels damaged or destroyed in the Mataafa Storm of November 27-29, 1905.
Her wreck has never been found — she remains one of Lake Superior's most sought-after undiscovered shipwrecks.
Lake sailors' lore holds that the Owen still reappears as a ghost ship in November snow squalls.
pois.visitTips: There is nothing to see here — and that is the point. This is deep, fully exposed open water east of Outer Island, the last place the Owen was seen afloat. The marker position is symbolic. Cross in settled weather only, and remember that November on this lake is no boater's season.
sources: Wisconsin Historical Society Shipwreck Database, 'Ira H. Owen (1887)'

pois.name: William E. Corey Stranding — Gull Island Shoal
pois.tagline: Where the brand-new flagship of the Pittsburgh fleet spent twelve days hard aground in the Mataafa Storm
pois.story:
When the Mataafa Storm exploded across Lake Superior on November 27, 1905, the William E. Corey was only a few months old — the largest and newest freighter in the Pittsburgh Steamship Company's steel fleet. Bound for Duluth, her captain ran for shelter among the Apostles, and the storm drove her hard onto Gull Island shoal, the shallow reef running off the little gull rookery northeast of Michigan Island.

Getting her off became one of the great salvage efforts in the islands' history: more than 150 men, four steamers, and three tugs worked the wreck for twelve days before the Corey finally floated free. No lives were lost, but the bill came to one hundred thousand dollars — serious money in 1905. The Corey's crew was lucky; the same storm took the Ira H. Owen and all nineteen of her men in the open water to the north.

The shoal kept snagging ships long after. In 1929 the Lighthouse Service finally planted a steel skeleton tower with an automatic acetylene light on Gull Island, tended by the keepers from Michigan Island — a belated answer to the reef that had humbled the biggest ship on the lakes.
funFacts: The Corey was just months out of the shipyard and the flagship-class vessel of the Pittsburgh Steamship Company when she stranded.
Freeing her took 150 men, four steamers, and three tugs working twelve days in the wake of the storm.
Gull Island's skeleton-tower light, lit September 30, 1929, cost $4,752 and was minded by the Michigan Island keepers.
pois.visitTips: Give this whole area a wide berth — Gull Island shoal is still a live hazard and the island itself is a protected nesting colony with a landing closure. Best appreciated through binoculars from safe water, imagining a 569-foot steel freighter pinned here in a November gale.

pois.name: Ontario — The Pulpwood Barge with a Whisky Legend
pois.tagline: The Apostles' last major shipwreck (1927) — 450 feet down off Outer Island, with ten cases of scotch in the story
pois.story:
The Ontario was an 1891-built Canadian vessel finishing her career as a humble tow barge, hauling pulpwood from Port Arthur, Ontario, to the mills at Ashland behind the tug Butterfield. On October 12, 1927, she left port with eleven hundred tons of pulpwood — and, the reports of the day said, ten cases of smuggled scotch, this being the dry heart of Prohibition. A high wind at departure built into a full gale on the open lake.

By early morning on October 13 the Ontario was beaten: taking water, boilers dead, no pumps, no steering. Waves tore away the lifeboat. At 2:55 a.m. the Butterfield caught her distress signals, hauled in the towline, and came alongside to pull four men off the sinking barge. The last man, Ernest Ludwig, caught a thrown lifeline, cut the towline as the deck went under him, fought the suction of the sinking hull, and was dragged aboard the tug by main strength. The Ontario went down ten minutes after her first distress signal — the last major shipwreck in the Apostle Islands.

For 85 years she was only a story. Then in the summer of 2012 a crew of veteran wreck hunters including Jerry Eliason found her about a mile and a half off Outer Island in roughly 450 feet of water — one of the deepest known wrecks in Lake Superior, buried in silt. Whether the scotch is still aboard, no one can say: state maritime archaeologists note that Prohibition-era smuggling claims attach to more than one Lake Superior wreck, and this one has never been verified.
funFacts: All five crewmen survived; Ernest Ludwig cut the towline himself as the barge sank beneath his feet.
At roughly 450 feet, the Ontario is considered one of the deepest located shipwrecks in Lake Superior.
The ten cases of smuggled scotch are documented as a contemporary report — tantalizing, but never confirmed.
pois.visitTips: The wreck lies far too deep for recreational diving and the exact position is not published — the marker is approximate. Passing boaters can raise a toast (a legal one) off Outer Island's east side; this is big, exposed water that turns dangerous fast in fall.

pois.name: Apostle Islands Indian Pageant Grounds (1924-25)
pois.tagline: A rain-soaked 1920s spectacle by Red Cliff Bay — four hundred Ojibwe performers, thirty-two mounted buglers, and a sixty-thousand-dollar flop
pois.story:
In the mid-1920s, Bayfield tourism boosters staged the most extravagant event in the region's history: the Apostle Islands Indian Pageant, performed in 1924 and 1925 in an outdoor amphitheater by Red Cliff Bay. Four hundred Ojibwe performers from the Red Cliff and Bad River bands, joined by additional actors and dancers, dramatized a loose version of regional history from 1634 to the mid-nineteenth century. The show opened with a parade of thirty-two mounted cavalry musicians and rolled on through staged battles and the landing of Marquette at Chequamegon Bay. Railroads offered special excursion fares, and 'alluring boat trips' aboard vessels like the Bruce — complete with the Northwoods Orchestra — stopped at Indian Pageant Park on their island tours.

The promoters dreamed of one hundred thousand visitors. The sky had other plans: in 1924 it rained on eighteen of the pageant's twenty-one performance days, and total attendance was just fifteen thousand. Twelve thousand came in 1925, and the pageant corporation ended the season sixty thousand dollars in debt. The NPS's own historians are blunt about the enterprise: it was more about exploiting the Ojibwe than assisting them, and whatever profits were imagined never reached the reservations.

In 1928 the grounds were sold to a Chicago group who built a hunting and fishing club, later home to the popular Pageant Tavern. The spectacle is gone, but the name survives on the map — Pageant Road still runs down toward the shore of Red Cliff Bay, a quiet reminder of the summer the whole Chequamegon region tried to become a stage.
funFacts: It rained on 18 of 21 performance days in 1924 — the weather effectively bankrupted the show.
Excursion boats listed 'Indian Pageant Park' as a scheduled stop alongside lighthouse and island tours.
The grounds' later incarnation, the Pageant Tavern, kept the name alive for decades, as does today's Pageant Road.
pois.visitTips: The site is on Red Cliff reservation land — please do not go ashore; view the Red Cliff Bay shoreline from the water (marker placed near the lake end of Pageant Road; the exact amphitheater footprint is not published). To engage with living Red Cliff Ojibwe culture, visit Frog Bay Tribal National Park or the Legendary Waters marina at Buffalo Bay.

pois.name: Herring King — Fire in East Bay
pois.tagline: The Boutin fish tug that was Sand Island's lifeline — burned to the waterline in 1917, then recycled into a cabin
pois.story:
No boat says 'herring era' like one actually named the Herring King. She began life as the fish tug Fish Hawk, and in the winter of 1909-10 was sawn in two, lengthened, and fitted with a gas engine salvaged from the vessel Superior — classic Bayfield thrift. Owned by the Boutin Fish Company and once touted as the fastest boat of her size on Chequamegon Bay, the 65-foot tug was Sand Island's connection to the world: she collected fish from the island camps for the Bayfield packing docks and carried lumber, groceries, and the mail to the families of East Bay.

Her end came on November 29, 1917, at the tail of the herring run. Returning from the Moe fishery on Sand Island, her gas engine backfired and ignited leaking fuel; fire swept the wooden hull in minutes, driving crewmen John Gordon and Clarence Russell to the bow as the packet steamer Goldish closed in. Russell reached a drifting, oarless lifeboat and was saved; Gordon went under a few feet short of a life buoy. The Herring King burned to the waterline with a thousand dollars' worth of fish aboard, and that evening fisherman Louis Moe towed the charred hull home to East Bay.

Islanders wasted nothing: summer resident Christian Aabel converted the burned-out hull into a cottage near today's East Bay dock, whose ruins still stand, and Burt Hill mounted the Herring King's bell on a pole beside his house, ringing it to call guests to meals — a dinner bell with a drowned man's story. She is the truest monument to November herring season: the three exhausting, dangerous weeks when boats came in listing under ten-ton lifts and the whole town of Bayfield, schoolchildren included, turned out to pick fish from the nets.
funFacts: A Bayfield County Press reporter aboard a herring tug in 1898 described decks so heaped with squirming herring the boat listed twenty degrees, forcing the crew to 'make another tack' and load the other side.
The Herring King delivered Sand Island's mail and groceries along with its fish — losing her was like losing the island's road to town.
Her charred hull served as the roof and walls of an island family's cabin near the East Bay dock, and her bell still stands by the old Hill place.
pois.visitTips: Land at the NPS East Bay dock on Sand Island and pair this story with a walk through the East Bay Norwegian settlement sites. Do not expect wreckage — the surviving traces are scant — but the shoreline where she was beached and reborn as a cabin is right here.

pois.name: Ashland Oredock Ruin
pois.tagline: The concrete backbone of a 1,800-foot ore dock — once the largest of its kind on the Great Lakes, saved in part by falcons
pois.story:
From the water off Ashland you can still read the city's iron age in one enormous concrete line: the base of the Soo Line (Wisconsin Central) ore dock, built 1916-18 to designs by the Toltz engineering firm of St. Paul, shipping its first ore in 1918. It rose on 6,800 driven piles, stood eighty feet above the waterline, and ran 900 feet with 150 ore pockets holding 52,500 tons; a 1925 extension stretched it to 1,800 feet. In its day it was the largest reinforced-concrete ore dock on the Great Lakes — a machine for pouring the Gogebic Range into the holds of freighters, wagonload by thundering wagonload.

The last Gogebic mine closed in 1965 and the dock fell silent. When the railroad moved to demolish the decaying giant in the late 2000s, the wrecking was famously interrupted in 2009 by three young peregrine falcons discovered nesting high in the steel and concrete — the birds stopped the work until they fledged. By 2013 the superstructure was down, but the massive base, roughly 1,800 feet long and 66 feet wide, was left standing and passed to the city.

Ashland has been turning the ruin into a public waterfront pier and park ever since, phase by phase, so people can once again walk out over Chequamegon Bay on the spine of the structure that built the town. Alongside the Ashland breakwater light, it is the most striking man-made landmark on the south shore of the bay.
funFacts: The demolition was halted in 2009 by nesting peregrine falcons — the chicks fledged before the wreckers returned.
The surviving concrete base is longer than any freighter that ever loaded at it — roughly 1,800 feet.
Some 6,800 piles were driven to carry the dock, which loomed 80 feet above the water when ore trains ran out on top.
pois.visitTips: Easily viewed by boat inside Chequamegon Bay — pair it with a pass by the Ashland Breakwater Light. Watch for construction zones and any posted keep-out buoys as the city continues converting the base into a public pier.
